h.select_rule: Keep hypotheses whose direction follows almost mechanically: condition on the edited field's own current value, or on a field that cuts off the edited part's input or output. Drop hypotheses relying on cross-field redundancy or competing effects. Keep diverse edit fields.
h.strategy: Favor the most reliable kinds of conditional effects. (1) Self-conditioning: an edit's effect depends most on what it replaces, so it is more positive when the parent's current value of that field is weak, empty or harmful, and more negative when the current value is strong. (2) Disconnection: an edit matters little when the edited part receives no input or cannot reach the output under the condition. (3) Floor and ceiling: gains are larger when the parent is poor overall and smaller when it is already near the best. Use cross-field redundancy only when the redundancy is near-total. Cover many different edit fields and values. Give a one-sentence mechanism for each.

hyps.why: Replacing an empty edge with a 3x3 conv adds a whole new information path, a much larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Filling a removed edge with a strong conv restores input to node 2, whereas replacing an existing op yields a smaller change.
Adding a 3x3 conv where there was no edge gives more gain than swapping it for another op.
A direct input-to-output conv path replacing nothing adds far more than replacing an existing op.
Replacing an absent edge with a strong conv is a larger improvement than replacing an existing op.
Edge 5 feeds the output directly, so replacing none with a conv gives a big gain.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 gets no input, so edge 2 carries nothing and editing it matters little.
Edge 4 starts at the disconnected node 1 when edge 0 is none, so a stronger op there has little effect.
Skipping from an input-less node 1 passes zeros, so the edit has almost no effect.
Node 1 is dead when edge 0 is none, so edge 2 edits are nearly irrelevant.
